clue.text: Calamitous change to Russia's old penny

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for the pre-decimal British penny (from Latin denarius)

indicators.note: change tells us to rework the letters of the words to Russia's into a new order

explanation.surface: Something dreadful has happened to an old Russian coin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change' makes ISASTROUS from the letters of TO RUSSIAS (the possessive S counts here), and D for the old penny goes in front. D was the symbol for the British penny before decimal coinage in 1971.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe events bringing ruin or catastrophe.

clue.text: Charge to student provokes fight

parts.note: a charge or fee owed is a due
L for learner, the plate a learner driver displays in Britain

explanation.surface: A bill landing on a student sparks a scuffle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'provokes' simply links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal combat between two people is a kind of fight.

clue.text: Stone fish

explanation.definitionFit: A sard is a reddish gemstone, and the Bible's sardine stone names it; the other sense is the small oily fish packed in tins.

clue.text: Mark my words, Sir, as he did once!

definitions.text: Mark my words, Sir, as he did once!

parts.words: Mark my words, Sir, as he did once!
parts.note: read as a teacher of old who marked his pupils' written work and was addressed as Sir by them

explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark my words' sounds like a warning, but here it is marking exercises; 'Sir' is how British pupils address a male teacher.
explanation.definitionFit: A male teacher in an old-fashioned school marked essays and was called Sir.

clue.text: To most Irish, 18 holes makes a game

parts.note: a round of golf is played over eighteen holes

indicators.note: most of the word means all but its last letter is kept

parts.note: Erse is an old name for the Irish Gaelic language

explanation.surface: Irish golfers reckon a full round of the course counts as sport.
explanation.walkthrough: '18' is a plain number here, not a cross-reference. ROUNDERS is a British bat-and-ball game, like a simpler baseball, played in schools.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a team sport with bat, ball and bases, popular in British schools.

clue.text: Peace-keeping type, but lacking benevolence

parts.note: the UN, the United Nations, sends peace-keeping forces
a type is a kind or sort

explanation.surface: A peacekeeper turns out to be a hard-hearted character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'but' just joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone unkind shows no goodwill or charity towards others.

clue.text: Article about present compiler is the last word

indicators.note: about means the article is wrapped round the other piece

parts.note: an is the indefinite article
the setter who is present refers to himself as me

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece about the crossword setter has the final say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' wraps the article round the setter's word for himself; setters often call themselves 'me' or 'I'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word closing a prayer or hymn is literally the final word said.

clue.text: 10 on vessel, say, accommodating this monkey?

indicators.note: say tells us the combined words are heard spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: the answer to 10 across, a Scot, is a Mac, put before a caique, a Levantine sailing boat

explanation.surface: A Scotsman aboard a boat seems to have a monkey with him.
explanation.walkthrough: '10' means the answer to 10 across, SCOT, giving MAC. 'say' makes MAC + CAIQUE (a small Turkish boat) sound like the monkey; 'accommodating' just pictures the boat carrying it.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an Old World primate, the rhesus being one example.

clue.text: Lowest form of anaesthetic doctors understood in Holy Writ

indicators.note: understood in means taken in or held within the other piece

parts.note: NT is the New Testament, part of Holy Writ
ether was an early general anaesthetic
MOs are medical officers, army doctors

explanation.surface: Doctors use the lowest grade of anaesthetic, as the Bible would have it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'understood in' means held inside the abbreviation for the New Testament; 'form of' only links the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: It means furthest down, the bottom-most level.

clue.text: It's no great shakes. Reynard may hope?

definitions.text: It's no great shakes. Reynard may hope?

parts.words: It's no great shakes. Reynard may hope?
parts.note: read 'no great shakes' ironically as huge shakings, and think of the fox hiding in its earth, whose ground might tremble

explanation.walkthrough: 'No great shakes' usually means mediocre, but here it is literal irony: tremors of the ground. A fox's den is called its earth, and Reynard is the traditional name for the fox.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a violent shaking of the ground caused by movement in the crust.

clue.text: Tax business concern in a small way

indicators.note: in tells us one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: St is the short form of street, a way written small
Co is the abbreviation for company, a business concern

explanation.surface: A tax on a small business firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts the firm inside the street abbreviation. SCOT is an old word for a tax, surviving in 'scot-free'.
explanation.definitionFit: In old England it was a levy or payment, hence escaping it was going scot-free.

clue.text: Course provider of rare stature represented outside university

indicators.note: outside means the rearranged letters go around the other piece
represented means the letters of rare stature are presented anew in another order

explanation.surface: A tall, rare figure from outside the university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'represented' rearranges RARE STATURE, and 'outside' puts it around U. 'Course' means a course of a meal, not of study.
explanation.definitionFit: A restaurant owner serves diners their dishes, a meal at a time.

clue.text: European accepts strange quest — rather like Alighieri

indicators.note: accepts means the first piece takes the second in

parts.note: a Dane is a European from Denmark

indicators.note: strange signals the letters of quest are put in an odd order

explanation.surface: A European takes on an odd quest, somewhat in the manner of the Italian poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange' rearranges QUEST to TESQU before 'accepts' puts it inside the Dane.
explanation.definitionFit: Dante Alighieri wrote the Divine Comedy; the adjective describes anything in his style.

clue.text: See London, perhaps

explanation.definitionFit: A metropolis is the seat of a metropolitan bishop, a see, and also a great capital city, of which the British capital is an example.

clue.text: Always> the first 26? Right, Hannah

parts.note: 26 across is LADY, and the first lady is Eve
Hannah More was an English writer and philanthropist of the 18th century

explanation.surface: A puzzle-solver trusts that the first lady answer is right, and credits the writer Hannah.
explanation.walkthrough: '26' refers to the answer to 26 across, so 'the first 26' is the first woman, Eve. The '>' after Always is an OCR mark.
explanation.definitionFit: It means for all time, forever.

clue.text: A number of pupils may do this in the cold

definitions.text: may do this in the cold

explanation.surface: Pupils are prone to doing this when they catch a chill.
explanation.definitionFit: A school class grouped by ability is a stream, and a runny nose with a cold flows or streams.

clue.text: Hide Roman, but outside the island

indicators.note: outside means the Latin word goes round the island

parts.note: sed is Latin for but
Crete is the large Greek island

explanation.surface: A Roman hides away, but not on the island itself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outside' wraps the Latin word round the island. The definition 'Hide' is present tense against a past-tense answer, a looseness as printed.
explanation.definitionFit: To conceal something is to stow it away out of sight.

clue.text: Such rubbish for a sports supervisor to employ!

parts.note: a referee, ref for short, supervises a match
to employ something is to use it

explanation.surface: A referee shouts that the decision is garbage.
explanation.definitionFit: It is household waste, garbage put out for collection.

clue.text: Sportsman occupied like Joseph Andrews's creator?

definitions.text: Sportsman occupied like Joseph Andrews's creator?

parts.words: Sportsman occupied like Joseph Andrews's creator?
parts.note: Henry Fielding wrote Joseph Andrews; a cricketer occupied in the field is said to be fielding, so he matches the novelist's name

explanation.walkthrough: Joseph Andrews is an 18th-century novel by Henry Fielding. In cricket, the side not batting is fielding.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket or baseball, a player stationed to stop and return the ball is so called.

clue.text: .Asks for engineers to initiate searches

indicators.note: to initiate means to come first, so this piece starts the word

parts.note: RE stands for the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
quests are searches or hunts for something

explanation.surface: Engineers asking to begin their search.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to initiate' makes the engineers' piece come first. The full stop before 'Asks' is OCR noise; the Royal Engineers are a British army corps.
explanation.definitionFit: It means politely seeks or solicits something.

clue.text: It's watertight, though cold, in' parts of Ushant

indicators.note: in signals one piece put inside another
parts of means the word Ushant is broken up and its letters rearranged

parts.note: taken as written: the island off Brittany
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: A ship off the coast of Brittany stays watertight despite the cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'parts of' rearranges USHANT to STAUNH, and 'in' puts C inside it before the H. Ushant is an island off the tip of Brittany.
explanation.definitionFit: Staunch, of a ship or container, means sound and leak-proof.

clue.text: In comedy he's too generous to hog the limelight

definitions.text: In comedy he's too generous to hog the limelight

indicators.note: In shows the letters are found within the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A comic's partner who never steals the show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' points inside HE'S TOO GENEROUS, where the letters run across three words. The whole clue also defines the comedian's foil.
explanation.definitionFit: A comic's straight-man partner is set up to feed lines and take the knocks.

clue.text: Puccini's first modern alternative to a leader of singing

indicators.note: first means the opening letter of the composer's name is taken

parts.note: modern means recent or new
or introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: The opera composer's first modern alternative to a choirmaster.
explanation.definitionFit: In a church or cathedral, this official leads the choir or congregation in chant.

clue.text: Architectural name for a barrier

parts.note: a dam is a barrier holding back water

explanation.surface: An architect's name for a wall that holds things back.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Adam was an 18th-century Scottish architect whose name labels a style of building and interior.
explanation.definitionFit: A famous Georgian designer of houses lent his surname to a style.

clue.text: Excursion just before the fall?

explanation.surface: An outing that ends in a tumble.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a short journey, and also the stumble that comes before someone falls over.

clue.text: She's not easy to hunt down in the pack…

definitions.text: She's not easy to hunt down in the pack

parts.words: She's not easy to hunt down in the pack
parts.note: read as the queen card in the three-card trick, find the ..., where the punter rarely finds her

explanation.walkthrough: 'Find the lady' is a street con with three cards; 'the pack' is not hounds but a deck of cards. The ellipsis leads on to 27.
explanation.definitionFit: In the trickster's game, the target card is the queen, a woman of rank.

clue.text: … and her true son could be from Florida

indicators.note: could be signals that the letters may be arranged into another form

explanation.surface: Continuing from 26, a woman's genuine son might come from Florida.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be' rearranges HER TRUE SON. The ellipsis ties this to the lady of 26.
explanation.definitionFit: A Floridian lives in the American South, so is a person of the southern states.

clue.text: Bellman's quarry loses direction in the Channel Islands

indicators.note: loses means a letter is dropped from the creature's name

parts.note: the Bellman leads the hunt for the Snark in Lewis Carroll's poem The Hunting of the Snark
N for north, a compass direction

explanation.surface: The prey of Carroll's Bellman goes astray among the Channel Islands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loses' takes the N out of SNARK. Sark is one of the Channel Islands, between England and France.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a small island in the archipelago, near Guernsey.

clue.text: Command of French in nonsense writer's joint

indicators.note: in means one piece is set within the other

parts.note: Edward Lear wrote nonsense verse, such as The Owl and the Pussycat
de is French for of
the hip is a joint

explanation.surface: Command of French in the joint of a nonsense poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' sets the French word inside the poet's name with its possessive S; Lear is famous for limericks.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in control or authority over others is to lead.
